# Don’t Call It a Decision Model

Nov 3, 2026

Jev makes **judgments**, code makes **decisions**.

###### *Allie Laabs, DevRel, TypeSafe*

We love that people have recognized the importance of the new category of models that Jev pioneered. It’s unsurprising that the term “decision models” has caught on as a name. When you first see Jev pick an option from a list, it’s easy to see it as making decisions. And indeed, we have used the word “decision” in our own education materials! So why is TypeSafe holding firm on calling Jev a System One model instead of a decision model? Let’s talk about it.

## It’s about where Jev fits in a system

Let’s break down what a typical system is, using the metaphor of circuits: inputs on the left (your data, application state, etc), they flow into logic, and then outputs on the right. Let’s use a simplified version of the Customer Service workflow from our [evals page](https://evals.typesafe.ai) as an example. The naive approach to using Jev in this workflow would be to place the entire *decision* in to a single Jev question:

When people first see Jev, this is how they imagine it fitting in to systems: give it all of your state, and have it make a *decision* about *what should happen*. This often looks like one big Choice question, and stuffing lots of semantic descriptions of business logic and caveats in to the `criteria` field.

While this *can* work, you will quickly find yourself engaging in what we call *prompt gymnastics*: tweaking these long explanations of conditions over and over to get each edge case handled. And then the next day you get some input you hadn’t thought of, the system fails, and you’re back to stuffing more caveats and clarifications in to criteria prose.

What’s happening here is trying to put intelligence at the wrong layer of abstraction. Your system already knows the criteria for each of your expected outcomes, and only some of it actually requires judgement. The rest is cold, hard logic:

When | Exit
reports an unauthorized charge | Fraud team: freeze & dispute
asks for a person, or threatens legal action | Hand to a person
wants money back, claim eligible, ≤ $25 | Refund now
wants money back, claim eligible, over $25 | Refunds team reviews
wants to cancel, subscription active, open to an offer | Offer to stay
otherwise | Answer & continue

So where does Jev fit in to this kind of system? To understand the answer, we need to peek inside to see what a *decision* is actually made of:

## Peel off the cap

Decisions in a system are rarely one atomic choice. Peel off the cap and we find wires running from the inputs through nodes of *code* and nodes of *judgment*. Decisions in software, workflows, and business are built this way. Checking “claim eligible, unpaid” is math. Answering “does the user want money back?” takes judgment. *That’s* where Jev belongs, and it’s exactly what we mean by System One: the quick intuitive judgments a knowledgeable person makes in seconds.

Code is great for answering what it can answer exactly. Jev answers only the small questions code can’t. Logic then combines those answers into the decision. It’s the combination of both judgement and code that allows a system to make reliable, observable decisions.

## Why Build It This Way

### 1. Clarity of design

Reliable systems require a clear understanding of how decisions are made. By decomposing decisions into their atomic judgments and logic paths, we gain clarity about what actually flows through the system, and what edge cases need to be handled.

### 2. Observability

In our all-in-one-judgment example from earlier, you’d write a single Choice stuffed with criteria:

```
{
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "state": {
    "conversation": "Customer: Hi, I'm not saying someone stole my card or anything, but t…",
    "account": "Ledger: txn-51a · Tucson Hardware Supply · $240.00 · Aug 14 · card pr…"
  },
  "questions": {
    "action": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "What should support do with this conversation?",
      "criteria": {
        "fraud_team": "The customer reports a charge, withdrawal, login, or account change they did not make or authorize. Pick this even if they also want a refund, ask for a person, or want to cancel.",
        "handoff_person": "The customer asks for a person, a manager, or a supervisor, or threatens legal action, a lawyer, or a regulator. Not if they report an unauthorized charge.",
        "instant_refund": "The customer wants money back, the refund claim on the account is eligible and not already refunded, and the amount is $25 or less. Not if they report an unauthorized charge or ask for a person.",
        "refunds_team": "The customer wants money back, the refund claim on the account is eligible and not already refunded, and the amount is over $25. Not if they report an unauthorized charge or ask for a person.",
        "retention_offer": "The customer wants to cancel, close, or downgrade, the subscription is active, and they would stay if something were offered or fixed. Not if any option above applies.",
        "answer": "None of the above. Answer the customer and continue the conversation, with no action on the account."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

When a case gets routed to an unexpected place, the only data you have about why is a single probability number. Which judgment mattered? Which rule? There’s nothing inside to read.

But take the cap off, and we get logs that read like this:

```
exit  fraud_team
  ├─ g_fraud    reports an unauthorized charge (p > 0.6)        true   ← decided
  ├─ g_person   asks for a person, or threatens legal action …  –
  ├─ g_instant  wants money back, claim eligible, amount ≤ $25  –
  ├─ g_large    wants money back, claim eligible, amount over…  –
  ├─ g_offer    wants to cancel, subscription active, open to…  –
  └─ else       answer                                          –
  judgments · Jev
       wants_money_back       0.99
       reports_unauthorized   0.94  ←
       requests_human         0.02
       threat_legal           0.01
       wants_to_cancel        0.02
       open_to_offer          0.22
  facts · your code
       refund_eligible       false
       small_refund          false
       subscription_active   false
```

Instead of “the model chose fraud\_team,” you get “the model made these six judgements, and here’s the logic path that followed.” The trace shows that `reports_unauthorized` sent it to the fraud team. Now we have real observable data to take action on. Was the judgment wrong, or the rule? The trace lets you tell, and the fix can be much more focused.

### 3. Extendability

Let’s say you suddenly have two new output paths, or thirty! When our system is designed with good decomposition, all you have to do is map out the logic for what would take those new paths, add any new judgments they require, and all of your existing carefully chosen judgments stay in place.

Here we see a new “Waive the fee” extension: one new judgment, one new code-computed fact, and the rest of the system stays in place. Because all Jev judgments are evaluated in isolation from one another, we don’t have to worry about new judgments having any impact on the ones we’ve already validated.

We invite you to try sketching the inside of one decision in your own app. Mark the lookups and arithmetic, then write a question next to each spot that needs judgment. [How to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one) covers decomposing questions and combining answers in code, and the [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns) show more ways to wire them.

Having trouble figuring out how to decompose the judgments in your own systems? Coding agents tend to be particularly good at understanding these kinds of systems! Try pointing your agent at this article and tell it to find places in your systems or code well suited for atomic judgments. And if you prefer a more human touch, please head on over to our [Discord](https://discord.gg/typesafe) where both our team and our community of builders would be happy to help out!

Jev makes judgments, code makes decisions.

## 4. Define Data and Provider Contracts Together

**Signature first.** Declare named inputs/outputs, optionality, arrays, constraints and descriptions with signature strings, `s()` or `f()`. Use schemas for shape, `addAssert()` for complete-output invariants and `addStreamingAssert()` for partial-output invariants. Reward scores are selection preferences, not hard validation. `fn()` gives host tools typed arguments/returns; handler authorization remains separate. Read [Signatures](references/signature.md), [Generators: Validation, selection, and hard guards](references/gen.md#validation-selection-and-hard-guards) and [Core agents: Tool Functions and Schemas](references/agent.md#tool-functions-and-schemas).

**Decision versus generation.** Jev supports required flat boolean/class/rubric score/Box outputs, not arbitrary numeric, optional/array/nested/freeform outputs or general tools. Native Noul/Choice/Score questions support advanced decision criteria. Compose a decision step with a generative provider for prose or a tool-using actor; pass typed decisions and evidence explicitly. Evidence provenance distinguishes native from elicited output, not guaranteed correctness or equal calibration across models. Validate thresholds/ranking on application data. Read [Typesafe: Evidence, provenance, and reranking](references/typesafe.md#evidence-provenance-and-reranking), Boolean/class signatures and adapter restrictions, and Native questions and application decisions.

**Atomic judgments, host policy.** Separate semantic questions from authoritative lookups/calculations, ordered rules and effect dispatch. Customer claims/model extractions are not system-of-record facts. Retain uncertainty and resolve or safely hold an uncertain higher-priority rule before choosing a lower-priority outcome, especially for overlapping intents. Read [Typesafe: Atomic judgments and host policy](references/typesafe.md#atomic-judgments-and-host-policy), then [26 architecture](examples/26-architecture.ts) case `26-architecture/evidence-aware-ticket`; selected threshold/applicability cases are linked from that specialist section.

| Provider choice | Design obligation | Specialist destination |

# Don’t Call It a Decision Model

Nov 3, 2026

Jev makes **judgments**, code makes **decisions**.

###### *Allie Laabs, DevRel, TypeSafe*

We love that people have recognized the importance of the new category of models that Jev pioneered. It’s unsurprising that the term “decision models” has caught on as a name. When you first see Jev pick an option from a list, it’s easy to see it as making decisions. And indeed, we have used the word “decision” in our own education materials! So why is TypeSafe holding firm on calling Jev a System One model instead of a decision model? Let’s talk about it.

## It’s about where Jev fits in a system

Let’s break down what a typical system is, using the metaphor of circuits: inputs on the left (your data, application state, etc), they flow into logic, and then outputs on the right. Let’s use a simplified version of the Customer Service workflow from our [evals page](https://evals.typesafe.ai) as an example. The naive approach to using Jev in this workflow would be to place the entire *decision* in to a single Jev question:

When people first see Jev, this is how they imagine it fitting in to systems: give it all of your state, and have it make a *decision* about *what should happen*. This often looks like one big Choice question, and stuffing lots of semantic descriptions of business logic and caveats in to the `criteria` field.

While this *can* work, you will quickly find yourself engaging in what we call *prompt gymnastics*: tweaking these long explanations of conditions over and over to get each edge case handled. And then the next day you get some input you hadn’t thought of, the system fails, and you’re back to stuffing more caveats and clarifications in to criteria prose.

What’s happening here is trying to put intelligence at the wrong layer of abstraction. Your system already knows the criteria for each of your expected outcomes, and only some of it actually requires judgement. The rest is cold, hard logic:

When | Exit
reports an unauthorized charge | Fraud team: freeze & dispute
asks for a person, or threatens legal action | Hand to a person
wants money back, claim eligible, ≤ $25 | Refund now
wants money back, claim eligible, over $25 | Refunds team reviews
wants to cancel, subscription active, open to an offer | Offer to stay
otherwise | Answer & continue

So where does Jev fit in to this kind of system? To understand the answer, we need to peek inside to see what a *decision* is actually made of:

## Peel off the cap

Decisions in a system are rarely one atomic choice. Peel off the cap and we find wires running from the inputs through nodes of *code* and nodes of *judgment*. Decisions in software, workflows, and business are built this way. Checking “claim eligible, unpaid” is math. Answering “does the user want money back?” takes judgment. *That’s* where Jev belongs, and it’s exactly what we mean by System One: the quick intuitive judgments a knowledgeable person makes in seconds.

Code is great for answering what it can answer exactly. Jev answers only the small questions code can’t. Logic then combines those answers into the decision. It’s the combination of both judgement and code that allows a system to make reliable, observable decisions.

## Why Build It This Way

### 1. Clarity of design

Reliable systems require a clear understanding of how decisions are made. By decomposing decisions into their atomic judgments and logic paths, we gain clarity about what actually flows through the system, and what edge cases need to be handled.

### 2. Observability

In our all-in-one-judgment example from earlier, you’d write a single Choice stuffed with criteria:

```
{
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "state": {
    "conversation": "Customer: Hi, I'm not saying someone stole my card or anything, but t…",
    "account": "Ledger: txn-51a · Tucson Hardware Supply · $240.00 · Aug 14 · card pr…"
  },
  "questions": {
    "action": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "What should support do with this conversation?",
      "criteria": {
        "fraud_team": "The customer reports a charge, withdrawal, login, or account change they did not make or authorize. Pick this even if they also want a refund, ask for a person, or want to cancel.",
        "handoff_person": "The customer asks for a person, a manager, or a supervisor, or threatens legal action, a lawyer, or a regulator. Not if they report an unauthorized charge.",
        "instant_refund": "The customer wants money back, the refund claim on the account is eligible and not already refunded, and the amount is $25 or less. Not if they report an unauthorized charge or ask for a person.",
        "refunds_team": "The customer wants money back, the refund claim on the account is eligible and not already refunded, and the amount is over $25. Not if they report an unauthorized charge or ask for a person.",
        "retention_offer": "The customer wants to cancel, close, or downgrade, the subscription is active, and they would stay if something were offered or fixed. Not if any option above applies.",
        "answer": "None of the above. Answer the customer and continue the conversation, with no action on the account."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

When a case gets routed to an unexpected place, the only data you have about why is a single probability number. Which judgment mattered? Which rule? There’s nothing inside to read.

But take the cap off, and we get logs that read like this:

```
exit  fraud_team
  ├─ g_fraud    reports an unauthorized charge (p > 0.6)        true   ← decided
  ├─ g_person   asks for a person, or threatens legal action …  –
  ├─ g_instant  wants money back, claim eligible, amount ≤ $25  –
  ├─ g_large    wants money back, claim eligible, amount over…  –
  ├─ g_offer    wants to cancel, subscription active, open to…  –
  └─ else       answer                                          –
  judgments · Jev
       wants_money_back       0.99
       reports_unauthorized   0.94  ←
       requests_human         0.02
       threat_legal           0.01
       wants_to_cancel        0.02
       open_to_offer          0.22
  facts · your code
       refund_eligible       false
       small_refund          false
       subscription_active   false
```

Instead of “the model chose fraud\_team,” you get “the model made these six judgements, and here’s the logic path that followed.” The trace shows that `reports_unauthorized` sent it to the fraud team. Now we have real observable data to take action on. Was the judgment wrong, or the rule? The trace lets you tell, and the fix can be much more focused.

### 3. Extendability

Let’s say you suddenly have two new output paths, or thirty! When our system is designed with good decomposition, all you have to do is map out the logic for what would take those new paths, add any new judgments they require, and all of your existing carefully chosen judgments stay in place.

Here we see a new “Waive the fee” extension: one new judgment, one new code-computed fact, and the rest of the system stays in place. Because all Jev judgments are evaluated in isolation from one another, we don’t have to worry about new judgments having any impact on the ones we’ve already validated.

We invite you to try sketching the inside of one decision in your own app. Mark the lookups and arithmetic, then write a question next to each spot that needs judgment. [How to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one) covers decomposing questions and combining answers in code, and the [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns) show more ways to wire them.

Having trouble figuring out how to decompose the judgments in your own systems? Coding agents tend to be particularly good at understanding these kinds of systems! Try pointing your agent at this article and tell it to find places in your systems or code well suited for atomic judgments. And if you prefer a more human touch, please head on over to our [Discord](https://discord.gg/typesafe) where both our team and our community of builders would be happy to help out!

Jev makes judgments, code makes decisions.

## Atomic judgments and host policy

Jev supplies semantic judgments; code owns authoritative facts/calculations, ordered rules and effects. Keep Choice/Score and Ax decision APIs for their typed contracts, but do not bury an entire business policy in one Choice. Model-extracted values and customer claims are not system-of-record facts: verify eligibility, balances, amounts, identity and current status against authenticated records, and calculate exact comparisons in code.

- Send bounded, relevant structured context with explicit source/field paths; separate customer assertions from verified records. Batch narrow, answer-independent questions over that context. “Independent” means no answer dependencies, not statistical independence, invariance after edits or a calibration guarantee. Questions needing another answer require a later call.
- Retain raw Noul probabilities through native answers or boolean evidence. Define a host-owned three-valued policy: yes above an evaluated upper boundary, no below a lower boundary, uncertain between them, with explicit inclusive/exclusive boundaries. A scalar boolean alone cannot retain that uncertainty. Missing required facts also need an explicit unresolved outcome.
- Evaluate multi-intent rules in priority order. For example: unauthorized-charge report → human/legal request → eligible refund → retention → ordinary answer. An uncertain higher-priority rule must trigger review, clarification or a defined safe hold before any lower-priority outcome; do not silently treat uncertainty as false. Dispatch authorized effects only after policy selection, separately from judgments and explanations.
- Optional applicability gate: pair a forced Choice with a companion Noul asking whether any supplied option applies. Ignore the Choice when inapplicable; preserve review when applicability is uncertain. Choice confidence alone does not establish applicability. Likewise, pair Box with a presence judgment and ignore its region unless presence passes policy.
- Optional speculative fan-out: ask answer-independent questions together even when only some branches will matter, then ignore irrelevant answers in code. Never let an irrelevant answer override a selected branch or authorize an effect.
- Optional composite scoring: use one Score rubric per dimension, normalize each by its own final rubric index, and apply explicit application weights in code. Preserve component scores/distributions. A weighted aggregate is an application score, not a joint-event probability; multiplying judgments does not establish one either.
- Keep privacy-aware traces with available model identity, question IDs/versions, raw probabilities, threshold/policy versions, evaluated rule IDs/order, selected/blocked outcome and fact source IDs/versions. Redact/minimize payloads and control access/retention; do not invent unavailable identities or log secrets to obtain observability.
- After changing wording, context, model, thresholds, rules or facts contracts, run targeted evaluation on representative labeled cases: uncertain boundaries, overlapping intents, missing/stale facts, inapplicable Choice, absent Box targets and effect denial. Re-evaluate affected judgments and end-to-end policy; no automatic correctness or calibration follows from decomposition.

Read [Don’t Call It a Decision Model](https://typesafe.ai/blog/dont-call-it-a-decision-model), [how to build with System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one), [confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence), and TypeSafe [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns) for [probability routing](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/probability-routing), [speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out) and [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring). Treat thresholds as workload-specific policies, not portable error-rate guarantees.

Selected examples: [26 architecture](examples/26-architecture.ts), `26-architecture/evidence-aware-ticket`; [06 decisions](examples/06-decisions.ts), `06-decisions/threshold-ownership` and `06-decisions/applicability-gate`. # Don’t Call It a Decision Model

Nov 3, 2026

Jev makes **judgments**, code makes **decisions**.

###### *Allie Laabs, DevRel, TypeSafe*

We love that people have recognized the importance of the new category of models that Jev pioneered. It’s unsurprising that the term “decision models” has caught on as a name. When you first see Jev pick an option from a list, it’s easy to see it as making decisions. And indeed, we have used the word “decision” in our own education materials! So why is TypeSafe holding firm on calling Jev a System One model instead of a decision model? Let’s talk about it.

## It’s about where Jev fits in a system

Let’s break down what a typical system is, using the metaphor of circuits: inputs on the left (your data, application state, etc), they flow into logic, and then outputs on the right. Let’s use a simplified version of the Customer Service workflow from our [evals page](https://evals.typesafe.ai) as an example. The naive approach to using Jev in this workflow would be to place the entire *decision* in to a single Jev question:

When people first see Jev, this is how they imagine it fitting in to systems: give it all of your state, and have it make a *decision* about *what should happen*. This often looks like one big Choice question, and stuffing lots of semantic descriptions of business logic and caveats in to the `criteria` field.

While this *can* work, you will quickly find yourself engaging in what we call *prompt gymnastics*: tweaking these long explanations of conditions over and over to get each edge case handled. And then the next day you get some input you hadn’t thought of, the system fails, and you’re back to stuffing more caveats and clarifications in to criteria prose.

What’s happening here is trying to put intelligence at the wrong layer of abstraction. Your system already knows the criteria for each of your expected outcomes, and only some of it actually requires judgement. The rest is cold, hard logic:

When | Exit
reports an unauthorized charge | Fraud team: freeze & dispute
asks for a person, or threatens legal action | Hand to a person
wants money back, claim eligible, ≤ $25 | Refund now
wants money back, claim eligible, over $25 | Refunds team reviews
wants to cancel, subscription active, open to an offer | Offer to stay
otherwise | Answer & continue

So where does Jev fit in to this kind of system? To understand the answer, we need to peek inside to see what a *decision* is actually made of:

## Peel off the cap

Decisions in a system are rarely one atomic choice. Peel off the cap and we find wires running from the inputs through nodes of *code* and nodes of *judgment*. Decisions in software, workflows, and business are built this way. Checking “claim eligible, unpaid” is math. Answering “does the user want money back?” takes judgment. *That’s* where Jev belongs, and it’s exactly what we mean by System One: the quick intuitive judgments a knowledgeable person makes in seconds.

Code is great for answering what it can answer exactly. Jev answers only the small questions code can’t. Logic then combines those answers into the decision. It’s the combination of both judgement and code that allows a system to make reliable, observable decisions.

## Why Build It This Way

### 1. Clarity of design

Reliable systems require a clear understanding of how decisions are made. By decomposing decisions into their atomic judgments and logic paths, we gain clarity about what actually flows through the system, and what edge cases need to be handled.

### 2. Observability

In our all-in-one-judgment example from earlier, you’d write a single Choice stuffed with criteria:

```
{
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "state": {
    "conversation": "Customer: Hi, I'm not saying someone stole my card or anything, but t…",
    "account": "Ledger: txn-51a · Tucson Hardware Supply · $240.00 · Aug 14 · card pr…"
  },
  "questions": {
    "action": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "What should support do with this conversation?",
      "criteria": {
        "fraud_team": "The customer reports a charge, withdrawal, login, or account change they did not make or authorize. Pick this even if they also want a refund, ask for a person, or want to cancel.",
        "handoff_person": "The customer asks for a person, a manager, or a supervisor, or threatens legal action, a lawyer, or a regulator. Not if they report an unauthorized charge.",
        "instant_refund": "The customer wants money back, the refund claim on the account is eligible and not already refunded, and the amount is $25 or less. Not if they report an unauthorized charge or ask for a person.",
        "refunds_team": "The customer wants money back, the refund claim on the account is eligible and not already refunded, and the amount is over $25. Not if they report an unauthorized charge or ask for a person.",
        "retention_offer": "The customer wants to cancel, close, or downgrade, the subscription is active, and they would stay if something were offered or fixed. Not if any option above applies.",
        "answer": "None of the above. Answer the customer and continue the conversation, with no action on the account."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

When a case gets routed to an unexpected place, the only data you have about why is a single probability number. Which judgment mattered? Which rule? There’s nothing inside to read.

But take the cap off, and we get logs that read like this:

```
exit  fraud_team
  ├─ g_fraud    reports an unauthorized charge (p > 0.6)        true   ← decided
  ├─ g_person   asks for a person, or threatens legal action …  –
  ├─ g_instant  wants money back, claim eligible, amount ≤ $25  –
  ├─ g_large    wants money back, claim eligible, amount over…  –
  ├─ g_offer    wants to cancel, subscription active, open to…  –
  └─ else       answer                                          –
  judgments · Jev
       wants_money_back       0.99
       reports_unauthorized   0.94  ←
       requests_human         0.02
       threat_legal           0.01
       wants_to_cancel        0.02
       open_to_offer          0.22
  facts · your code
       refund_eligible       false
       small_refund          false
       subscription_active   false
```

Instead of “the model chose fraud\_team,” you get “the model made these six judgements, and here’s the logic path that followed.” The trace shows that `reports_unauthorized` sent it to the fraud team. Now we have real observable data to take action on. Was the judgment wrong, or the rule? The trace lets you tell, and the fix can be much more focused.

### 3. Extendability

Let’s say you suddenly have two new output paths, or thirty! When our system is designed with good decomposition, all you have to do is map out the logic for what would take those new paths, add any new judgments they require, and all of your existing carefully chosen judgments stay in place.

Here we see a new “Waive the fee” extension: one new judgment, one new code-computed fact, and the rest of the system stays in place. Because all Jev judgments are evaluated in isolation from one another, we don’t have to worry about new judgments having any impact on the ones we’ve already validated.

We invite you to try sketching the inside of one decision in your own app. Mark the lookups and arithmetic, then write a question next to each spot that needs judgment. [How to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one) covers decomposing questions and combining answers in code, and the [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns) show more ways to wire them.

Having trouble figuring out how to decompose the judgments in your own systems? Coding agents tend to be particularly good at understanding these kinds of systems! Try pointing your agent at this article and tell it to find places in your systems or code well suited for atomic judgments. And if you prefer a more human touch, please head on over to our [Discord](https://discord.gg/typesafe) where both our team and our community of builders would be happy to help out!

Jev makes judgments, code makes decisions.
